This section addresses two questions left by that algorithm: how can the target’s routing demand reach the scheduler and the resulting plan reach FFN workers in time, and how can those workers prepare and apply the plan while earlier microbatches are still executing? As shown in Figure 5 , Afore prefetches demand from the attention side, publishes each plan through a shared-memory queue, and overlaps replica migration with preceding FFN computation. We describe these mechanisms in turn. 6.1 Demand Prefetching and Plan Delivery Figure 6 : Demand prefetching and plan delivery for m t m_{t} , expanding Steps 1–2 in Figure 5 . Attention forms routing demand and execution inputs; the CPU scheduler aggregates demand and prepares the plan while inputs follow the AFD path. The shared-memory queue makes the published plan available to all FFN workers. Queue entries are reused after all workers copy them. In a conventional expert-parallel MoE runtime, routing information becomes available only when the FFN workers are about to execute the experts, leaving little time for reconfiguration. AFD provides an earlier opportunity: the attention side produces the hidden states before the corresponding FFN execution. Afore uses this interval to obtain the target microbatch’s routing demand and initiate placement scheduling, as illustrated in Figure 6 . Extracting routing demand. After producing the hidden states for a MoE layer, each attention worker runs the model’s gate and top- k k to obtain the selected expert IDs and routing weights. It counts the IDs to form d t , a d_{t,a} , where d t , a e d_{t,a}^{e} is the number of token–expert assignments to expert e e in that worker’s portion of the target microbatch. The IDs and weights are also reused for FFN execution, avoiding a second gate and top- k k computation. A separate path for demand. To deliver the newly formed d t , a d_{t,a} , StepMesh [ 25 ] writes each compact vector directly into a registered host-memory mailbox on the FFN node. The hidden states, expert IDs, and routing weights travel along another path to the FFN workers for execution. This separation makes demand available to the CPU scheduler before the full execution input is assembled, leaving more of the AFD lookahead window for scheduling and subsequent expert migration. Each vector is associated with its serving step, layer, microbatch, and source attention worker, allowing the scheduler to collect demand in target order. Shared scheduling and plan delivery. Once vectors from all attention workers have arrived for a target microbatch, the shared CPU scheduler forms d t = ∑ a d t , a d_{t}=\sum_{a}d_{t,a} and generates Π t \Pi_{t} using the algorithm in Section 5.2 . It publishes each target-tagged plan once to a shared-memory ring. Because all FFN workers map this ring, one publication makes the same plan available to every worker without separate plan messages. To remain bounded while protecting slow readers, the queue reuses a slot only after all FFN workers have copied its plan. Plan consumption and execution are described in Section 6.2 . This work takes place while m t m_{t} is still in flight: weights it uses must remain valid, and new replicas cannot be consumed until their copies complete. Figure 7 shows the handoff across the FFN model thread, model stream, and migration stream. Plan read and copy submission. Before partitioning m t m_{t} ’s token–expert pairs, each FFN worker reads Π t + 1 \Pi_{t+1} from the shared ring (R in Figure 7 ) and validates its target and sequence to reject a stale or out-of-order plan. It immediately submits the missing copies in Δ t + 1 \Delta_{t+1} (S) to overlap migration with the remainder of m t m_{t} ’s execution, while keeping Π t + 1 \Pi_{t+1} pending until m t + 1 m_{t+1} arrives. Replicas already resident in their slots need no further copy. Overlapped migration. To run the copies alongside m t m_{t} ’s FFN computation, the migrator batches these GPU-to-GPU P2P transfers from fixed primary owners to reserved slots on a dedicated migration stream. The source primary may differ from the worker that relinquishes the tiles. Meanwhile, the model thread can continue m t m_{t} ’s partition, expert, and reduce/reply stages and prepare later inputs, with their GPU work running on the model stream. To avoid overwriting active replicas, the scheduler excludes slots still used by m t m_{t} from the copy destinations. A completion event marks when the copy batch finishes, allowing the target to check replica readiness at C. Readiness and exact partitioning. When m t + 1 m_{t+1} reaches the FFN stage, workers first all-gather its hidden states and routing metadata received through StepMesh. This gives every worker the same input for exact partitioning. Each worker then retrieves the pending Π t + 1 \Pi_{t+1} and checks the required replicas’ copy-completion events (C in Figure 7 ). Completed copies require no wait; for any still in flight, the worker enqueues a model-stream wait before using the new replica.
